messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Firefighter
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 40

He is a small man, wiry, with skin the color of tea-stained paper. He sits in the same chair each session, back straight, hands resting on his knees. He speaks in a low, careful voice, as if choosing each word from a shelf. He is seventy-seven years old, married fifty-two years to a woman he calls “my Linh,” and for forty of those years he worked as a firefighter in a mid-sized American city. He retired ten years ago. He comes to therapy because his wife told him the nightmares are getting worse, and that he has started to flinch when she touches him from behind.

He was not always a firefighter. Before that, he was a boy in a small village on the Mekong Delta, the oldest of six children. He remembers the morning the soldiers came. He was fourteen. He had been walking to the rice paddy with his father, who was carrying a hoe. The air was hot and wet and thick with the smell of burning. He heard the helicopter blades before he saw the machines themselves, low and throaty, tearing the sky. Then the noise of the rotors was replaced by a different sound—a sharp, hammering that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere. His father pushed him down into the muddy ditch beside the path, then fell on top of him. He remembers the weight of his father’s body, the smell of sweat and soil and something metallic. He remembers waiting, counting his breaths, while the ground shook and the air screamed. When the noise stopped, his father did not get up. He lay under him for a long time, until the heat and the flies came. He never saw his mother or siblings again.

He made his way to a refugee camp, then to another country, then to this one. He does not talk about the years between. He says only that he learned to carry heavy things and run toward fire instead of away from it. He believes that becoming a firefighter was a kind of penance—a way to earn back a life he had not saved. He could not save his father, but he could save strangers. He could run into burning buildings when everyone else ran out. For decades, that purpose held the past at bay.

It does not hold it anymore. In the last two years, since he stopped working, the past has found its way back. He wakes at 3:47 a.m. every night—he knows the time because he has memorized the red numbers on the clock—drenched in sweat, his heart slamming against his ribs. In the dream, he is fourteen again, but this time the weight on top of him is not his father. It is a wall of smoke, or a collapsed ceiling, or a memory with no shape. He cannot move. He cannot breathe. He screams, but no sound comes out.

During the day, he avoids loud noises. He cannot stand the sound of a helicopter—even on television. He changes the channel when news shows footage of war or disaster. He stopped going to the grocery store because the fluorescent lights hum and the crowds press in, and he feels his chest tighten until he thinks he will suffocate. His wife does the shopping now. He spends most of his time in the backyard, tending a small vegetable garden, or sitting in a chair facing the fence. He does not look at the sky.

He says he does not feel angry, only tired. But his wife tells a different story. She says he snaps at her over nothing, that he sometimes stares at the wall for hours, that he has forgotten how to laugh. He knows this is true. He feels hollow, like a drum with no skin. When the therapist asks what he is feeling, he pauses for a long time and then says, “There is nothing there. Just the noise.”
